forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets' auditors now expect a clean accounts opinion by 2028/29 at the earliest, not 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets Council's external auditor, EY, now expects the earliest date for a fully unqualified opinion on the council's accounts to be 2028/29, two years later than the 2026/27 the council had aimed for. An addendum to EY's 2025/26 audit plan, put to the Audit Committee on 24 September 2026, says the earlier target is "premature". It says updated audit guidance (LARRIG 06) is "in part outdated".

The 2025/26 audit will examine only the closing balances on the balance sheet. The full audit of income and spending, and of the balance sheet, is deferred to 2026/27. EY expects to gain assurance over unusable reserves, such as the pension reserve, by the end of 2025/26. For usable reserves, the part the council can actually spend, it says "it will take a few years".

A briefing paper to the committee says the council's progress is "behind the expected timescales" set out in the national recovery guidance (LARRIG 01), because "limited procedures were completed for 2023/24 and 2024/25". That prevented a move on from a disclaimer opinion, where auditors give no opinion at all. The briefing links this to a significant weakness and a statutory recommendation on the council's arrangements for financial reporting. It notes that 87% of local government bodies met the earlier deadlines for producing statements, but that "quality and completeness – not speed" held back audit progress.

The pension fund papers show a related problem. EY issued a disclaimer on the £1,620m present value of promised retirement benefits in 2024/25. Its reports have recorded errors in the membership data given to the actuary every year since 31 March 2019. The fund has engaged external consultants to correct the data, and EY is testing the results. The outcome is not yet confirmed.

For 2025/26 the base audit fee is £91,183, still to be confirmed. EY lists modified opinions among the factors that could add work. The fund's net assets were £2,192m at 31 March 2025, including £355m of unquoted investments valued on management judgement. Both the Corporate Director, Resources, and the Head of Pensions and Treasury are interim appointments.

findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement preparation process improved, with one significant weakness addressed.
findings.detail: In 2024/25, Ernst & Young identified a significant weakness in the Annual Governance Statement process, noting it was prepared by the Head of Internal Audit which compromised independence. For 2025/26, responsibility was transferred to the Corporate Strategy Team with revised formal review and challenge arrangements. Ernst & Young concluded the revised process is more consistent with CIPFA guidance and provides a more balanced and transparent assessment of governance challenges.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council can make governance improvements when required; however, this remains one area of progress amid multiple other continuing significant weaknesses, and sustainability depends on continued embedding.
findings.figures: 1 significant weakness lifted from 2024/25 to 2025/26 (AGS preparation)
findings.quote: Based on the evidence available at the date of this report, we are satisfied that the Council has addressed the significant weakness identified in 2024/25.

findings.headline: £7.8m of 2026/27 required savings reported at risk and £4.1m unlikely to be delivered against £69.8m total requirement
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget identified £69.8 million of required savings. By Period 2, £29.2 million had been achieved (primarily pension reduction) and £28.7 million was reported on track, representing 83% either delivered or on track. However, £7.8 million was reported as at risk and £4.1 million as unlikely to be delivered. Further, the Period 2 Budget Monitoring Report forecasts a net overspend of £19.2 million, which is not reflected in the reserves forecast position.
findings.matters: If planned savings are not delivered, the council will face further budget gaps on top of already forecast deficits; the ability to deliver major savings plans is uncertain given track record of recurring overspends.
findings.figures: £69.8 million total required savings (2026/27); £29.2 million achieved; £28.7 million on track (83% total); £7.8 million at risk; £4.1 million unlikely to be delivered; £19.2 million net overspend forecast Period 2
findings.quote: £29.2 million had been achieved, primarily relating to the pension reduction, and a further £28.7 million was reported as on track. This represented 83% of savings being either achieved or on track, with £7.8 million reported as at risk and £4.1 million reported as unlikely to be delivered.

findings.headline: Revised Minimum Revenue Provision policy defers capital financing costs to future years, reducing budget flexibility from 2050 onwards.
findings.detail: The Council changed its MRP policy in 2024/25 to charge capital financing costs disproportionately toward later years of asset life. This delivered a £7.7 million short-term benefit to the General Fund in 2025/26 (charged £3.96 million against £11.7 million budget), but Ernst & Young concluded this does not represent a prudent approach. The Council acknowledged that by 2059/60, the existing budget will no longer be sufficient. Without this policy change, the council would face additional pressures of up to £27 million across the medium-term financial plan to 2028/29.
findings.matters: Deferring capital costs is a short-term fix that disguises underlying deficits rather than addressing them; it increases future borrowing requirements and reduces flexibility to respond to future shocks.
findings.figures: 2025/26 MRP charge £3.96 million against budget of £11.7 million (£7.7 million saving); £27 million additional pressure across MTFS 2026-29 without policy change; existing budget insufficient by 2059/60
findings.quote: We have concluded that the application of the Council's revised MRP policy did not represent a prudent approach, resulting in MRP charges being profiled disproportionately towards the later years of an asset's economic life.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer role held by four different individuals in 18 months, with no permanent holder at time of report.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer role has been subject to interim arrangements throughout most of the review period and has been held by four different individuals in permanent, temporary and interim capacities within 18 months. Although the Council subsequently completed recruitment and appointed a permanent Section 151 Officer, interim covering arrangements remained in place at the date of the report.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer is responsible for financial strategy, control and reporting; instability in this critical role during a period of major financial pressures and governance failures undermines financial leadership and suggests difficulty retaining experienced finance staff.
findings.figures: 4 different Section 151 Officers in 18-month period; no permanent holder at report date
findings.quote: At the date of this report, the role remains subject to interim arrangements and has been held by four different individuals, in permanent, temporary and interim capacities, within an 18-month period.

findings.headline: Housing Regulator assigned C3 consumer grading for serious failings in safety, quality and accountability standards.
findings.detail: Following self-referral to the Housing Ombudsman, the Regulator of Social Housing issued its first regulatory judgement on 30 April 2025, assigning a C3 consumer grading, the lowest rating. The Regulator found serious failings in how the Council is delivering consumer standards with particular concerns in the Safety and Quality Standard and weaknesses in Transparency and Accountability. The Council does not expect to seek reassessment before mid-2027. Housing and Regeneration has also reported £20.8 million overspend in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Major regulatory failure in social housing indicates failures in service delivery, governance and regulatory compliance; housing is a significant part of council responsibilities and the associated overspend worsens financial position.
findings.figures: C3 consumer grading (30 April 2025); £20.8 million Housing and Regeneration overspend (2025/26); reassessment not expected before mid-2027
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing confirmed a consumer grading of C3, reporting serious failings in how the Council is delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards, with significant improvement required.
